title: IV. The Lost Dog
paragraphs: Kolya leaned against the fence with an air of dignity, waiting for Alyosha to appear. Yes, he had wanted to meet him for a long time. He had heard a great deal about him from the boys, but until now he had always put on a look of disdainful indifference whenever Alyosha's name came up, and had even “criticized” what he heard about him. Secretly, though, he longed to make his acquaintance; everything he'd been told about Alyosha struck him as sympathetic and attractive. So this moment mattered: to begin with, he had to show himself at his best, to show his independence. “Otherwise he'll think of me as thirteen and take me for a boy, like the rest of them. And what are these little boys to him? I'll ask him once I know him. It's a pity I'm so short, though. Tuzikov is younger than I am, yet he's half a head taller. But I have a clever face. I'm not good-looking. I know I'm ugly, but I've got a clever face. I mustn't talk too freely; if I fall into his arms all at once, he may think — pah, how horrible if he should think — !”

Such were the thoughts that kept Kolya on edge while he did everything he could to look as independent as possible. What distressed him most was being so short; his “ugly” face bothered him less than his height. A year earlier he had made a pencil mark on the wall at home in one corner to show his height, and every two months since then he had anxiously measured himself against it to see how much he had gained. But alas — he was growing very slowly, and this sometimes reduced him almost to despair. His face was in fact by no means “ugly”; on the contrary, it was rather attractive, with fair, pale skin dusted with freckles. His small, lively gray eyes had a fearless look and often lit up with feeling. He had rather high cheekbones, small, very red but not very full lips, and a small, unmistakably turned-up nose. “I've got a regular pug nose, a regular pug nose,” Kolya used to mutter when he caught sight of himself in the mirror, always turning away indignantly. “Or maybe I don't even have a clever face?” he sometimes wondered, doubting even that. But it should not be supposed that his mind was preoccupied with his face and height. On the contrary, however bitter the moments in front of the mirror were, he quickly forgot them, and forgot them for a long time, “giving himself up entirely to ideas and to real life,” as he put it to himself.

Alyosha came out quickly and hurried up to Kolya. Before he reached him, Kolya could see that he looked delighted. “Can he really be so glad to see me?” Kolya wondered, pleased. Let us note in passing that Alyosha's appearance had changed completely since we last saw him. He had given up the cassock and was now wearing a well-cut coat and a soft, round hat, and his hair had been cropped short. It all suited him; he looked quite handsome. His charming face always carried a good-humored expression, but there was a gentleness and serenity in that good humor. To Kolya's surprise, Alyosha came out just as he was, without an overcoat. He had obviously come in a hurry. He held out his hand to Kolya at once.
“So here you are at last! How anxious we've been to see you!”
“There were reasons you'll know about in a moment. In any case, I'm glad to meet you. I've long hoped for the chance, and I've heard a great deal about you,” Kolya muttered, a little breathless.
“We were bound to meet anyway. I've heard a lot about you too; but you've taken a long time coming here.”
“Tell me, how are things going?”
“Ilusha is very ill. He's certainly dying.”
“How awful! You must admit medicine is a fraud, Karamazov,” Kolya cried warmly.

“Ilusha has spoken of you often — very often, even in his sleep, in his delirium, you know. One can see you used to be very, very dear to him ... before that incident ... with the knife. Then there's another reason ... Tell me, is that your dog?”
“Yes, Perezvon.”
“Not Zhutchka?” Alyosha looked at Kolya with eyes full of pity. “Is she lost forever?”

“I know you'd all like it to be Zhutchka. I've heard all about it.” Kolya smiled mysteriously. “Listen, Karamazov, I'll tell you everything. That's what I came for; that's why I asked you to come out here — to explain the whole business to you before we go in,” he began eagerly. “You see, Karamazov, Ilusha started in the preparatory class last spring. Well, you know what our preparatory class is like — a pack of small boys. They began teasing Ilusha at once. I'm two classes higher up, of course, so I only watched them from a distance. I could see the boy was weak and small, but he wouldn't give in; he fought back. I saw he was proud, and his eyes were full of fire. I like children like that. And they teased him all the more. The worst of it was that he was dressed horribly at the time — his breeches were too small for him, and there were holes in his boots. They tormented him about it; they jeered at him. I can't stand that. I stood up for him at once and gave them a real hiding. I beat them up, and yet they adore me, do you know that, Karamazov?” Kolya boasted impulsively. “I'm always fond of children. I've got two little chicks in my hands at home right now — that's what held me up today. So they stopped beating Ilusha, and I took him under my protection. I could see the boy was proud. I'm telling you, the boy was proud. But in the end he became slavishly devoted to me; he'd do the smallest thing I asked, obeyed me as though I were God, tried to imitate me. In the breaks between classes he'd run to me at once, and I'd spend time with him. On Sundays too. People always laugh when an older boy takes up with a younger one like that, but that's a prejudice. If it's my fancy, that's enough. I'm teaching him, developing him. Why shouldn't I develop him if I like him? Here you are, Karamazov, you've taken up with all these little nestlings — I see you want to influence the younger generation, to develop them, to be of use to them, and I'll admit, this trait in your character, which I knew by hearsay, attracted me more than anything. But let's get to the point. I noticed a certain softness and sentimentality coming over the boy, and you know I have a positive hatred of this sheepish sentimentality — I've hated it since I was a baby. There were contradictions in him, too: he was proud, but he was slavishly devoted to me, and yet all at once his eyes would flash and he'd refuse to agree with me; he'd argue, fly into a rage. I sometimes put forward certain ideas just to see, and I could tell it wasn't that he disagreed with the ideas so much as that he was simply rebelling against me, because I was cool in response to his affection. And so, in order to train him properly, the tenderer he became, the colder I became. I did it on purpose — that was my plan. My aim was to form his character, to knock him into shape, to make a man of him ... and besides ... no doubt you understand me at a word. All of a sudden I noticed he was downcast and dejected for three days in a row — not because of my coldness, but for some other reason, something more serious. I wondered what the tragedy was. I dug it out of him and found out he'd somehow gotten to know Smerdyakov, who was footman to your late father — this was before his death, of course — and Smerdyakov had taught the little fool a stupid trick — that is, a brutal, nasty trick. He told him to take a piece of bread, stick a pin in it, and throw it to one of those hungry street dogs that snap up anything without chewing it, and then watch what happened. So they prepared a piece of bread like that and threw it to Zhutchka, that shaggy dog there's been all this fuss about. The people of the house that owned her never fed her, though she barked all day. (Do you like that stupid barking, Karamazov? I can't stand it.) So she lunged at the bread, swallowed it, and began to yelp; she spun around and ran off, yelping as she went, until she was out of sight. That was Ilusha's own account. He confessed it to me and cried bitterly. He hugged me, shaking all over. He kept repeating, ‘She ran away yelping, she ran away yelping' — the sight of it haunted him. He was tormented by remorse; I could see it. I took it seriously. I decided to give him a lesson, for other things as well. So I must confess I wasn't altogether straightforward — I pretended to be more indignant than I really was. ‘You've done a nasty thing,' I said. ‘You're a scoundrel. I won't tell on you, of course, but I'll have nothing more to do with you for a while. I'll think it over and let you know through Smurov' — that's the boy who's come with me just now; he's always ready to do anything for me — ‘whether I will have anything to do with you in the future or whether I give you up for good as a scoundrel.' He was tremendously upset. I'll admit I felt as I was speaking that I'd gone too far, but there was no helping it. I did what I thought best at the time. A day or two later I sent Smurov to tell him I'd stopped speaking to him. That's what we call it at school when two boys refuse to have anything more to do with each other. Secretly, I only meant to send him to Coventry for a few days and then, if I saw signs of repentance, hold out my hand to him again. That was my intention. But what do you suppose happened? He heard Smurov's message, his eyes flashed. ‘Tell Krassotkin from me,' he cried, ‘that I'll throw bread with pins in it to all the dogs — all of them, all of them!' ‘So he's going in for a little temper,' I thought. ‘We must smoke it out of him.' And I started treating him with contempt; whenever we crossed paths I'd turn away or smile sarcastically. And just then that business with his father happened. Do you remember? You have to realize he was already horribly worked up by everything that had happened. The boys, seeing I'd given him up, turned on him and taunted him, shouting, ‘Wisp of tow, wisp of tow!' He was soon in regular fights with them, which I'm very sorry for. Apparently they gave him one very bad beating. One day he flew at them all as they were coming out of school. I stood a few yards off, watching. And I swear, I don't remember laughing; quite the opposite — I felt terribly sorry for him, and in another minute I'd have run up to take his side. But then he suddenly met my eyes. I don't know what he imagined, but he pulled out a penknife, rushed at me, and jabbed at my thigh — right here, on my right leg. I didn't move. I don't mind admitting I'm brave sometimes, Karamazov. I just looked at him contemptuously, as if to say, ‘So this is how you repay all my kindness? Do it again, if you like — I'm at your service.' But he didn't stab me again; he broke down, frightened at what he'd done, threw the knife away, burst into tears, and ran off. Of course I didn't snitch on him, and I made all the other boys keep quiet so it wouldn't reach the masters' ears. I didn't even tell my mother until the wound had healed up. And the wound was nothing — a scratch. Then I heard that the same day he'd been throwing stones and had bitten your finger — but you understand now the state he was in! Well, it can't be helped: it was stupid of me not to go and forgive him — that is, make it up with him — when he was taken ill. I'm sorry for it now. But I had a special reason. So now I've told you the whole thing ... though I'm afraid it was stupid of me.”

“Oh, what a pity,” Alyosha exclaimed with feeling, “that I didn't know sooner what terms you two were on — I'd have come to you long ago to beg you to go to him with me. Would you believe it, when he was feverish he talked about you in his delirium. I had no idea how much you meant to him! And you really haven't managed to find that dog? His father and the boys have been hunting for it all over town. Would you believe it, since he's been ill, I've three times heard him repeat with tears, ‘It's because I killed Zhutchka, father, that I'm ill now. God is punishing me for it.' He can't get that idea out of his head. And if the dog could be found and shown to be alive, you might almost think the joy would cure him. We've all been pinning our hopes on you.”
“Tell me, what made you hope I'd be the one to find her?” Kolya asked with great curiosity. “Why count on me rather than anyone else?”

“There was a rumor that you were looking for the dog and that you'd bring her once you found her. Smurov said something of the kind. We've all been trying to persuade Ilusha that the dog is alive, that she's been spotted. The boys brought him a live hare; he just glanced at it with a faint smile and asked them to set it free in the fields. So we did. His father has only just come back with a mastiff puppy, hoping to comfort him that way; but I think it only makes things worse.”
“Tell me, Karamazov, what sort of man is the father? I know him, but how do you see him — as a mountebank, a buffoon?”

“Oh no. There are people of deep feeling who have somehow been crushed. In them, buffoonery becomes a kind of resentful irony against people they don't dare tell the truth to, from years of being humiliated and intimidated by them. Believe me, Krassotkin, that sort of buffoonery is sometimes tragic in the extreme. His whole life now is wrapped up in Ilusha, and if Ilusha dies, he'll either go mad with grief or kill himself. I'm almost certain of it when I look at him now.”
“I understand you, Karamazov. I see you understand human nature,” Kolya added with feeling.
“And as soon as I saw you with a dog, I thought you were bringing Zhutchka.”

“Wait a bit, Karamazov — perhaps we'll find her yet; but this is Perezvon. I'll let him go in now, and maybe he'll cheer Ilusha up more than the mastiff puppy. Hang on, Karamazov, in a minute you'll see something. But — I say — I'm keeping you standing out here!” Kolya cried suddenly. “You don't even have an overcoat on in this bitter cold. You see what an egoist I am. Oh, we're all egoists, Karamazov!”
“Don't worry about that. It is cold, but I don't catch cold easily. Let's go in, though. And, by the way, what's your name? I know you're called Kolya, but what else?”
“Nikolay — Nikolay Ivanovitch Krassotkin, or, as they say in official documents, ‘Krassotkin, son of.'” Kolya laughed for some reason, but then added suddenly, “Of course I hate the name Nikolay.”
“Why?”
“It's so trite, so ordinary.”
“You're thirteen?” Alyosha asked.

“No, fourteen — or rather, I'll be fourteen very soon, in a fortnight. I'll confess one weakness of mine, Karamazov, to you alone, since this is our first meeting, so you can understand my character right away. I hate being asked my age, more than hate it ... and on top of that ... there's a libelous story going around about me — that last week I played robbers with the preparatory boys. It's true that I did play with them, but it's a complete libel to say I did it for my own amusement. I have reason to believe you've heard the story; but I wasn't playing for my own amusement, I was doing it for the children, because they couldn't think up anything to do by themselves. But there's always some silly tale going around. This is an awful town for gossip, I can tell you.”
“But what if you had been playing for your own amusement — what's wrong with that?”
“Come on — for my own amusement? You don't play horses, do you?”

“You should look at it this way,” Alyosha said, smiling. “Grown-up people go to the theater, and there they watch the adventures of all sorts of heroes — sometimes robbers and battles too — and isn't that just the same thing, in another form? And young people's games of soldiers or robbers in their play time are also art in its first stage. You know, they spring from the growing artistic instincts of the young. And sometimes these games are much better than theater performances; the only difference is that in the theater people go to watch the actors, while in these games young people are the actors themselves. But that's only natural.”

“You think so? Is that your view?” Kolya looked at him intently. “You know, that's a rather interesting idea. When I go home I'll think it over. I'll admit, I thought I might learn something from you. I've come to learn from you, Karamazov,” Kolya concluded, his voice full of spontaneous feeling.
“And I from you,” Alyosha said, smiling and pressing his hand.
Kolya was thoroughly pleased with Alyosha. What struck him most was that Alyosha treated him exactly like an equal and talked to him as if he were “quite grown up.”
“I'll show you something in a moment, Karamazov — a theatrical performance too,” he said, laughing nervously. “That's why I've come.”
“Let's go first to the people of the house on the left. All the boys leave their coats there, because the room is small and hot.”

“Oh, I'm only coming in for a minute. I'll keep my overcoat on. Perezvon will stay here in the passage and be dead. _Ici_, Perezvon, lie down and be dead! You see how he's dead. I'll go in first and scout it out, then I'll whistle to him when I think it's the right moment, and you'll see — he'll come charging in like mad. Only Smurov mustn't forget to open the door at the right moment. I'll arrange it all, and you'll see something.”
